title: These Chairs Grew on Trees (Really!)
summary:
What if you could pick a chair from a tree like an apple? In Derbyshire, England, Gavin and Alice Munro are doing just that. They own Full Grown, a company that grows furniture from living trees.

Here's how it works. They plant young trees and let them grow for about five years. Then they cut them back to the stumps so new shoots grow. This is called coppicing. They bend the new branches around metal frames shaped like chairs or tables. The branches are grafted, or joined together, so they grow into one solid piece. After years of growing, the furniture is harvested and left to dry for about a year. Then it's sanded and polished smooth.

The Munros mostly use willow trees, but also oak, ash, cherry, and apple. Their method uses only about 25 percent of the energy needed to make a wooden chair in a factory. No heavy machines — just sunlight, soil, water, and time. Plus, the "Furniture Field" is a safe home for birds and other wildlife.

Tree shaping isn't new. Ancient Greeks, Egyptians, and Chinese did something similar. But the Munros have taken it to a whole new level.
why_it_matters: It shows that everyday things like chairs can be made in gentler ways — with sunlight, soil and patience instead of heavy machines — and that slow ideas can still be very clever.

background_read: Derbyshire is a county in the middle of England, known for its green hills and countryside.
Coppicing is an old farming trick: cutting trees low so they grow lots of straight new branches, and people have used bendy willow branches for baskets and fences for hundreds of years.
Tree shaping is thousands of years old — ancient Greeks, Egyptians and Chinese grew trees into useful or beautiful shapes long before Full Grown started growing chairs.
Article_Structure: WHO: Gavin and Alice Munro, the couple who own the company Full Grown
WHAT: They grow chairs and tables from living trees instead of building them in factories
WHERE: In Derbyshire, England, in a place called the 'Furniture Field'
WHY: Their slow method uses only about 25 percent of the energy of factory furniture making, and it gives birds and other wildlife a safe home

perspectives.description: They love that Full Grown's furniture uses far less energy and that the field provides a home for birds and other wildlife.
They might say these chairs cost a lot and take many years to grow, so they can't replace factory furniture for most families.
They note that tree shaping is ancient, but the Munros turn an old craft into a modern business that people can actually buy from.
